Guided Inquiry

1 · The electron that started it all

This is Davisson & Germer's 1927 experiment. Electrons accelerated through 54 V carry a de Broglie wavelength λ = h/√(2mK) = 1.67 × 10⁻¹⁰ m — the same order as the nickel atomic spacing d = 2.15 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, so the two markers on the ruler nearly coincide. The scattered intensity peaks where d sin θ = λ, at θ ≈ 51°: the 50° maximum they measured, from a wavelength no particle was supposed to have.

2 · Predict — what about a cricket ball?

A 0.15 kg cricket ball moves at a few m/s. Its wavelength λ = h/p is compared with the ball. How big is λ relative to the ball?

3 · The cricket ball, on the same ruler

The Particle selector now reads Cricket ball. The λ marker has dived to the far-left end of the ruler while the obstacle marker (the ball itself) sits near the right end — the gap readout puts ~32 orders of magnitude between them on a log scale. The scattering curve collapses to a single forward spike: a geometric shadow, no fringes, for any obstacle you could build.

4 · The rule that made both pictures

Same equation, same simulation, two wildly different pictures — because λ = h/p is universal but the RATIO λ/size is not. When λ ≈ size the wave nature is visible; when λ ≪ size it is unmeasurable but still real. Try the proton and dust grain to see the whole spectrum. Increase the kinetic energy on any particle: notice λ halves whenever KE quadruples (λ ∝ 1/√KE).

The Physics

de Broglie Waves — Why You Never See a Cricket Ball Diffract · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A beam of one kind of particle is aimed at a row of obstacles, and the sim puts the particle's wavelength next to the obstacle's size on a single log ruler. It lets you compare the two for objects from an electron to a cricket ball.

What you'll learn

  • How a particle's de Broglie wavelength depends on its mass and its kinetic energy.
  • What Davisson and Germer measured in 1927, and how the condition d sin θ = λ turns it into a wavelength.
  • How to read a wavelength against an obstacle's size on a log ruler.
A gun fires particles at a row of atoms a distance d apart. A detector arc measures how many leave at each angle θ from the normal.

What's on screen

  • λ marker (blue) on a ruler running from 10⁻³⁵ m to 1 m.
  • Obstacle marker (amber) on the same ruler.
  • Apparatus (lower left): the gun, the row of atoms and the detector arc.
  • Scattering plot (lower right): intensity against angle, with a tag naming the regime.
  • The two numbers panel: the wavelength λ and the ratio λ/size.
See itStart from the 54 eV electron and the nickel spacing. Watch for: the blue λ marker and the amber obstacle marker on the ruler, and a peak in the scattering plot.

03

A moving particle has the wavelength λ = h/p

de Broglie's relation links a particle's wavelength λ to its momentum p, with h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s:

λ = h / p = h / (mv)
Momentum p = mv for a particle of mass m and speed v.

The sim sets a kinetic energy K instead of a speed. For speeds well below c, K = p²/(2m), so p = √(2mK) and

λ = h / √(2mK)

The default electron has K = 54 eV = 8.65 × 10⁻¹⁸ J and m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg. That gives p = 3.97 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m/s, a speed of 4.36 × 10⁶ m/s, and λ = 1.67 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Here K is only 10⁻⁴ of the rest energy mc², so the non-relativistic form is safe.

See itOpen the two-numbers panel for the 54 eV electron. Watch for: λ = 1.67 × 10⁻¹⁰ m in the panel, matching the blue marker's label on the ruler.
04

Davisson and Germer saw electron waves scatter

In 1927 they fired electrons accelerated through 54 V at a nickel crystal. The electrons did not scatter evenly. They showed a clear maximum near 50° from the normal.

Treat the surface atoms as a row with spacing d = 2.15 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Waves scattered at angle θ add up when the extra path d sin θ is a whole number n of wavelengths:

d sin θ = nλ   (n = 1)
The sim draws the first-order maximum, at ±θ.

With λ = 1.67 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, sin θ = λ/d = 0.776, so θ = 50.9°. Run it backwards: d sin 50° = 1.65 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, within about 1.5 % of h/√(2mK). A wave had been measured for a particle.

The sim uses one row at normal incidence. A real nickel crystal is three-dimensional, so this is the simple version of the idea.

See itLook at the scattering plot for the 54 eV electron. Watch for: a dashed line and the label Bragg peak: sin θ = λ/d, θ ≈ 50.9°.
05

Wavelength falls as the square root of mass and energy

Since λ = h/√(2mK), λ ∝ 1/√K at fixed m, and λ ∝ 1/√m at fixed K. Four times the energy, or four times the mass, halves λ. A hundred times the energy divides it by 10.

For the electron, K = 216 eV (four times 54 eV) gives λ = 0.83 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, and the Bragg angle drops from 50.9° to 22.8°.

λ depends on momentum, so a heavy particle can match a light one. The sim's proton opens at K = 0.0259 eV, roughly thermal energy at room temperature. Its λ = 1.78 × 10⁻¹⁰ m is about the electron's, though it is 1836 times heavier. For the same momentum, a heavier particle needs a smaller K, since K = p²/(2m).

See itRaise the electron's K from 54 eV to about 216 eV. Watch for: λ falling to about 0.83 × 10⁻¹⁰ m and the Bragg peak moving to about 22.8°.
06

Wave effects show when λ is near the obstacle size

Diffraction depends on the ratio λ/size, not on λ alone. When λ is comparable to the obstacle, the wave spreads and gives clear maxima. When λ is far smaller, the wave goes almost straight on and leaves a shadow. The wave is still there, but its effect is too small to measure.

At the sim's opening values:

Particleλobstacleλ/size

Dust grain, 5 × 10⁻²² J6.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ m1 µm6.6 × 10⁻¹⁰
Cricket ball, 0.51 J1.7 × 10⁻³³ m7 cm2.4 × 10⁻³²

Even the smallest obstacle on the slider, 10⁻¹⁵ m, is about 6 × 10¹⁷ times wider than the ball's λ.

See itSwitch to the cricket ball. Watch for: the blue λ marker at the far left of the ruler, a ratio near 10⁻³², and a forward spike with no side peaks.
07

Where it matters

  • Electron microscopes. Electrons at 100 keV have λ ≈ 3.7 × 10⁻¹² m, about a hundred thousand times shorter than visible light (≈ 5 × 10⁻⁷ m), so the wave limit on detail is far finer.
  • Crystal structure. Electrons and thermal neutrons have λ near 10⁻¹⁰ m, the same as atomic spacings, so crystals diffract them. A neutron at 25.9 meV has λ = 1.78 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.
  • Everyday objects. A cricket ball bowled at 40 m/s still has λ = 1.1 × 10⁻³⁴ m, so no fringes ever show up.
Go deeper

For fast particles the true momentum is above √(2mK). At 100 keV the sim's formula gives 3.88 × 10⁻¹² m, about 5 % above the relativistic value 3.70 × 10⁻¹² m, which is why it warns at large K.

08

Summary

In one line. A moving particle's de Broglie wavelength is set by its momentum, and the sim lets you set that wavelength against the size of an obstacle.

Key points

  • λ = h/p = h/√(2mK) for speeds well below c.
  • Four times K, or four times m, halves λ.
  • d sin θ = λ gives the first Bragg maximum, θ = 50.9° for the 54 eV electron.
  • The ratio λ/size decides whether wave effects can be seen.

Common mix-ups

  • "Only electrons have a de Broglie wavelength." Every moving object has one, from λ = h/p. For large objects it is far too small to detect.
  • "The heavier the particle, the shorter the wavelength." λ depends on momentum. A slow proton can have the same λ as a faster electron.
  • "A tiny λ means the wave has disappeared." The relation still holds. Its effects are just far smaller than any obstacle can show.

Things to try on your own

  • Choose the electron, raise K by a factor of 100 (two units on the log slider), and check that λ falls to a tenth.
  • Choose the proton and raise K until the Bragg angle is about 30°.
  • Choose the cricket ball and drag the obstacle to its smallest size. Read the ratio.
